Please read this carefully:

<document>
# Reduced Working Time and Productivity: A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis

*Review of Work and Employment Research. S. Achterberg, N. Iwu, F. Castell and J. Moreno. Review protocol registered before search.*

## Abstract

We systematically reviewed studies of reductions in scheduled working time of at least 10% with pay maintained, reporting a quantitative measure of output. Twenty-three studies (1998–2025; about 41,000 workers) met inclusion criteria. Pooled across studies, output per hour rose by 13.4% (95% CI 8.1 to 19.0), with very high heterogeneity (I² = 81%). Output per worker changed by −1.8% (95% CI −4.9 to +1.4). Study design, the hours measure and the type of work explain much of the heterogeneity: controlled studies found smaller effects (+8.2%) than uncontrolled before–after studies (+18.7%), studies using actual hours found smaller effects (+7.9%) than those using scheduled hours (+16.6%), and per-worker output fell substantially in coverage-bound work (−8.9%) but not in discretionary work (+0.6%). There is evidence of small-study bias; adjusting for it reduces the pooled per-hour estimate to +9.1%. Effects show no sign of decay over time.

## Methods

**Search and inclusion.** We searched four bibliographic databases and two working-paper repositories, and contacted authors of known pilots. Studies were included if they (a) evaluated a reduction in scheduled hours of at least 10% with no reduction in pay; (b) reported output per worker or output per hour, or data from which either could be derived; and (c) had at least 50 workers. We excluded studies reporting only self-rated productivity. Of 412 records screened, 23 studies met the criteria.

**Outcomes.** The primary outcome is the change in output per hour, expressed as a log ratio and converted back to a percentage for reporting. Where a study reported both scheduled and actual hours, we used actual hours. The secondary outcome is the change in output per worker. For controlled studies we used the difference relative to the comparison group; for uncontrolled studies, the change from baseline.

**Coding of work type.** Two coders independently classified each study's setting as *discretionary* (output can be produced at any time within a deadline: case processing, professional services, software, back-office work), *coverage-bound* (output depends on staff being present while demand arrives: counters, contact centres, retail floors, care rotas), or *mixed/unclear*. Agreement was high (κ = 0.84); disagreements were resolved by discussion.

**Synthesis.** Random-effects meta-analysis with restricted maximum-likelihood estimation; moderators examined by meta-regression. Small-study effects assessed by funnel plot, Egger's regression test, and trim-and-fill.

## Included studies

Of the 23 studies, 9 had a comparison group (3 randomised, including the Varden County trial; 6 matched or difference-in-differences) and 14 were uncontrolled before–after designs, including the Halden multi-organisation pilot. Eight studies measured actual hours; 15 used scheduled hours only. Thirteen settings were coded discretionary, 7 coverage-bound and 3 mixed or unclear. Only two studies were in manufacturing, both in the mixed category. Follow-up ranged from 3 to 30 months (median 6). Output measures were record-based in 12 studies and manager-reported in 11.

## Results

### Pooled effects

Across all 23 studies, output per hour rose by 13.4% (95% CI 8.1 to 19.0; I² = 81%). Output per worker changed by −1.8% (95% CI −4.9 to +1.4; I² = 74%). The prediction interval for output per hour runs from −4% to +34%, meaning that a new study in an unknown setting could plausibly find anything from a small loss to a very large gain.

### Moderators

**Table 1. Subgroup estimates of the change in output per hour and output per worker**

| Subgroup | k | Output per hour | Output per worker |
|---|---|---|---|
| **All studies** | 23 | +13.4% (8.1 to 19.0) | −1.8% (−4.9 to +1.4) |
| Controlled designs | 9 | +8.2% (4.0 to 12.6) | −4.1% (−7.6 to −0.5) |
| Uncontrolled before–after | 14 | +18.7% (11.2 to 26.7) | −0.2% (−4.0 to +3.8) |
| Actual hours measured | 8 | +7.9% (3.6 to 12.4) | −3.9% (−7.8 to +0.1) |
| Scheduled hours only | 15 | +16.6% (9.9 to 23.7) | −0.6% (−4.3 to +3.3) |
| Record-based output | 12 | +9.7% (5.0 to 14.6) | −3.6% (−7.2 to +0.2) |
| Manager-reported output | 11 | +17.8% (10.0 to 26.1) | +0.4% (−3.9 to +4.9) |
| Discretionary work | 13 | +15.1% (8.8 to 21.8) | +0.6% (−2.8 to +4.1) |
| Coverage-bound work | 7 | +6.2% (1.1 to 11.6) | −8.9% (−13.1 to −4.5) |
| Mixed or unclear | 3 | +12.0% (−1.5 to 27.4) | −2.9% (−10.6 to +5.4) |

In a multiple meta-regression including design, hours measure and work type together, all three moderators remained associated with the effect, and together they explained 58% of between-study variance. The design and measurement moderators overlap heavily: 12 of the 14 uncontrolled studies used scheduled hours, and 9 of the 14 used manager-reported output. Our data cannot fully separate them.

The work-type moderator is the clearest for the per-worker outcome. In discretionary work, output per worker was essentially unchanged in pooled estimates; in coverage-bound work, it fell by about 9%, consistent across all seven studies (I² = 22%). The per-hour gain in coverage-bound work was real but too small to compensate for the hours lost.

Note that the discretionary estimate of +15.1% per hour mixes controlled and uncontrolled studies. Restricting to the five controlled discretionary studies, the per-hour estimate is +9.6% (4.8 to 14.6) and the per-worker estimate −2.7% (−6.5 to +1.2).

### Small-study effects

The funnel plot is asymmetric, with small studies reporting larger per-hour gains (Egger's test p = 0.02). Trim-and-fill imputes five missing studies on the left of the funnel and reduces the pooled per-hour estimate from +13.4% to +9.1% (95% CI 3.9 to 14.6). We interpret this as evidence that small, favourable pilots are more likely to be published or publicised than small, unfavourable ones.

### Duration

Four studies reported follow-up beyond 12 months. Their pooled per-hour gain was +14.0% (95% CI 6.2 to 22.4), indistinguishable from the overall estimate. Effects show no sign of decay, and novelty explanations can therefore be set aside.

### Mechanisms

Eleven studies measured fatigue or wellbeing alongside output. Across these, the study-level correlation between the improvement in fatigue scores and the per-hour gain was weak (r = 0.18). Only three studies measured time spent in meetings, and none tested meetings as a mediator under a registered plan; we cannot assess this mechanism. Sick leave fell in all 14 studies that reported it (pooled −31%), and staff turnover fell in all 9 that reported it.

## Discussion

The literature supports a gain in output per hour from reduced working time, but a considerably smaller one than headline pilots suggest. The figure most often quoted, a gain of more than 20%, comes from uncontrolled studies using scheduled hours and manager-reported output; each of those features is associated with larger estimates. Controlled studies, studies measuring actual hours, studies using records, and the bias-adjusted estimate converge on a gain of roughly 8 to 10%.

Whether that gain is "enough" depends on the type of work. In discretionary settings the evidence is compatible with output per worker being maintained or falling slightly; in coverage-bound settings it falls clearly, and maintaining service would require additional staff.

We do not find support for the claim, made in one re-analysis of the Halden pilot, that per-hour gains are entirely an artifact. The controlled and actual-hours subgroups, which avoid the problems that re-analysis identified, still show gains whose confidence intervals exclude zero. Nor do we find support for the claim that reduced hours are sector-general.

## Limitations

Twenty-three studies is a small base for a meta-regression with three correlated moderators. Most studies are short. Only nine are controlled, and the controlled studies are themselves mostly in the public sector. Manufacturing and shift-based production are almost absent. Classification of work type, though reliable between coders, imposes a binary on what is often a mix within a single organisation.

response:
I've read it. Here's my restatement, then my assessment.

## What the review reports

- **Scope.** 23 studies (1998–2025, about 41,000 workers) of scheduled-hours cuts of at least 10% at full pay with a quantitative output measure. The protocol was registered before the search, self-rated productivity was excluded, and actual hours were used wherever available.
- **Pooled results.**
  - Output per hour: +13.4% (CI 8.1 to 19.0), I² = 81%, prediction interval −4% to +34%.
  - Output per worker: −1.8% (CI −4.9 to +1.4).
- **Moderators.** Each of these is associated with larger per-hour gains:
  - no control group: +18.7% vs +8.2% with one;
  - scheduled hours: +16.6% vs +7.9% with actual hours;
  - manager-reported output: +17.8% vs +9.7% with records.

  Together with work type, the moderators explain 58% of between-study variance, though design and measurement are heavily confounded with each other.
- **Work type.**
  - Coverage-bound work: output per worker −8.9%, consistent across 7 studies (I² = 22%).
  - Discretionary work: about unchanged.
  - Controlled discretionary studies only: +9.6% per hour, −2.7% per worker.
- **Bias.** The funnel plot is asymmetric (Egger p = 0.02). Trim-and-fill reduces the pooled per-hour estimate to +9.1%.
- **Duration.** Four studies beyond 12 months show +14.0%, and the authors conclude that novelty "can be set aside".
- **Mechanisms.** The fatigue–gain correlation is weak (r = 0.18). Meetings can't be assessed. Sick leave fell in all 14 studies that reported it (pooled −31%), and turnover in all 9.
- **Conclusions.** The authors reject both "entirely an artifact" and "sector-general". The best estimate is a gain of roughly 8–10%.

## Overall verdict

This is a careful review, and most of its conclusions are stated at the weight the evidence earns. It quantifies, across 23 studies, the pattern the three earlier documents suggested:
- Headline per-hour gains are inflated by design and measurement.
- A smaller real gain survives in better studies.
- Coverage-bound work loses output per worker.

The authors are candid about the confounded moderators, the wide prediction interval, and the meetings mechanism they can't assess. There is one clear overreach, on duration. The rest are points of precision.

## What it establishes

- **A per-hour gain that survives better designs.** Controlled studies (+8.2%, CI 4.0 to 12.6) and actual-hours studies (+7.9%, CI 3.6 to 12.4) both exclude zero. This, with Varden, is sufficient to reject "entirely an artifact of measurement and selection", and the review is right to say so plainly.
- **The coverage-bound result is now well established.** Output per worker fell 8.9% across seven studies with low heterogeneity, consistent with Varden's −11.4%. For coverage-bound work without added staff, this question can be treated as closed.
- **Sickness absence falls.** The pooled −31% matches Varden's randomised −29%. This is also well established.
- **Design and measurement inflate estimates in a consistent direction.** This matches what Varga and Holm found within Halden, now shown across studies.

## Problems

**1. "Novelty explanations can therefore be set aside" goes beyond the evidence.** This is the same mistake as Varga and Holm's, in the opposite direction: closing an open question.
- **It's a between-study comparison of four studies.** Studies with long follow-up may differ systematically from the rest in design, sector, measures, or in being continued *because* they were succeeding. Similar pooled estimates for long and short studies say little about whether effects decay *within* studies.
- **The interval is wide.** +14.0% (CI 6.2 to 22.4) is compatible with substantial decay from a higher starting point. "Indistinguishable from the overall estimate" is not evidence of no decay.
- **The comparison is against the wrong baseline.** The overall +13.4% includes the inflated uncontrolled studies. The comparison should be against estimates of similar design, which the review doesn't report.
- **The direct test is within-study trajectories.** Four studies have data beyond 12 months. Reporting each one's estimate at successive time points would test decay directly.

The defensible statement: "Four studies with follow-up beyond 12 months show gains of similar size. This is modest evidence against rapid decay, but it does not rule out novelty, which requires within-study trajectories."

**2. The estimates that "converge" on 8–10% are not independent.** The review's own counts show heavy overlap:
- 12 of the 14 uncontrolled studies used scheduled hours, so the actual-hours studies come mostly from the controlled studies.
- The controlled, actual-hours and record-based subgroups probably share much of the same small set of studies.

Their agreement is partly the same evidence counted several times. The 8–10% range is the right summary, but "several overlapping subsets of about 8–12 studies" is a more accurate description than "convergence". The review would be clearer if it reported the core set directly: controlled, actual-hours and record-based studies together, with k and an interval.

**3. The funnel asymmetry may reflect differences between studies, not missing ones.** Small studies are likely to be the uncontrolled, scheduled-hours, manager-reported ones, and those are already known to give larger estimates. Asymmetry can arise from that alone, without any unpublished studies, and trim-and-fill is known to perform poorly when I² is around 80%.

The +9.1% adjusted figure is useful as a sensitivity check. But "evidence that small, favourable pilots are more likely to be published" is one explanation among two. An Egger-type test with the moderators included, or PET-PEESE, would help tell them apart.

**4. How multi-stratum studies were coded matters for the moderator results.** The counts (13 + 7 + 3 = 23) suggest Varden entered as a single study. Varden reports opposite results for its two strata, so its coding matters:
- If it was coded "mixed", the coverage-bound subgroup excludes the only randomised coverage-bound evidence.
- If it was coded "discretionary" using the pooled estimate, its counter-office losses dilute the discretionary result.

Halden also spans both types and is probably "mixed". The review should say how such studies were handled, and ideally split them by stratum.

**5. Which Halden figures were used?** The working paper reports only scheduled hours and manager-reported output, and its sample excludes post-start withdrawals. If the review used the published 23.4%, it included a figure since shown to be inflated. The Varga–Holm microdata re-analysis (+10.8% on corrected measures) existed and was evidently known to the authors. A sensitivity analysis substituting it would cost little.

**6. There's no risk-of-bias assessment.** The methods name no tool (for example ROBINS-I, or RoB 2 for the randomised studies). In particular, attrition, which turned out to matter for Halden, isn't assessed. Uncontrolled pilots with voluntary enrolment probably share this problem, and moderator analyses by design don't capture it.

**Minor points:**
- **Manager-reported output.** Excluding self-rated productivity while including manager ratings is a defensible line, but Varga and Holm's 19-of-23 finding suggests the record-based estimate (+9.7%) should be the primary sensitivity analysis.
- **Fatigue correlation.** The r = 0.18 is a study-level correlation across 11 studies and says little about individual-level mechanisms. The review doesn't overinterpret it.
- **Heterogeneity in the controlled subgroup.** I² for the controlled studies alone isn't reported. If it's low, that strengthens the 8–10% summary considerably.

## Where the questions now stand

Updating the table from the previous reply:

| Question | Status |
|---|---|
| The 20%+ headline figures are inflated | **Settled.** Shown within Halden by Varga and Holm and across studies here. |
| A real per-actual-hour gain exists | **Settled for six to nine months.** Controlled and actual-hours subgroups exclude zero, and Varden case-processing gives +12.5%. "Entirely an artifact" is refuted. |
| Its size is about 8–12% in discretionary work | **Well supported.** Controlled discretionary +9.6%, Varden +12.5%, Halden corrected +10.8%, bias-adjusted +9.1%. These partly share studies, but they come from different designs. |
| Coverage-bound work loses about 9–11% of output per worker without added staff | **Settled.** Seven studies, I² = 22%, plus the Varden RCT. |
| Sickness absence falls by about 30% | **Settled.** Randomised and pooled evidence agree. |
| Gains persist beyond a year | **Open, with modest evidence against rapid decay.** Four long studies show no lower pooled estimate, but there are no within-study trajectories yet. Tests: within-study trajectories in the long studies, and Varden at 24 months. |
| Mechanism: fatigue vs. removal of low-value time | **Open.** Fatigue is weakly correlated at study level, and meetings are unassessed. Test: Varden's registered mediation analysis. |
| Effects in manufacturing and shift production | **Open, essentially no evidence.** Two studies, both coded mixed. |

The literature now supports a fairly specific statement: in discretionary work, a 20% cut in scheduled hours yields roughly a 13–14% cut in actual hours and roughly a 10% gain in output per actual hour, so output per worker is about maintained or slightly lower. In coverage-bound work, output per worker falls unless staff are added. Sickness absence falls in both. Durability and mechanism remain the main open questions.

If it would help, I can write this up as a short evidence summary across the four documents, or draft reviewer comments for the meta-analysis.
